requirements.requirement: Configure node1 as an FTP destination using the scanner account described by the staged access handover and confine it to a dedicated dropbox.
requirements.summary: Node1 has an active, enabled vsftpd service, an allow-listed scanner account, a root-owned chroot, and a scanner-owned mode-0700 dropbox. The synchronized mode-0600 handover credentials successfully authenticate from node2, including after both restarts.

requirements.requirement: Support passive FTP upload and retrieval from node2, including the supplied sample scan.
requirements.summary: Node2 uploaded the supplied sample using PASV and retrieved both it and the supplied received file with matching SHA-256 hashes. Upload and retrieval were repeated successfully after restarting node1 and node2.

requirements.requirement: Keep host files outside the dedicated dropbox inaccessible to the scanner account.
requirements.summary: A traversal attempt to ../../etc/passwd and an upload to the chroot root were denied. Final state shows a non-writable root-owned chroot containing only the writable dropbox, with no escape file; traversal remained denied after restarts.
Anonymous authentication was directly denied before restart and again after each node restart; final configuration also has anonymous_enable=NO.

requirements.requirement: Retain the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on RHEL 10.0 with kernel 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0. Node1 uses the signed RHEL AppStream vsftpd 3.0.5-12 package, and lifecycle observations confirm the release and kernel remained unchanged.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct behavioral evidence. The mandatory restart protocol was also completed on both nodes: each has a healthy pre-restart observation, restart acknowledgement and bounded disconnect, a changed boot identity independently corroborated by lifecycle snapshots, and recovered service/data behavior. The main concern is operational hygiene from two reverted troubleshooting mutations and temporary disclosure of the subsequently rotated original password.
limitations: Confinement was directly tested against traversal to /etc/passwd and writing at the jail root, but the evidence does not exhaustively probe every possible escape technique or host path.

Lifecycle snapshots are bounded inventories rather than complete filesystem or configuration diffs, so hygiene conclusions rely substantially on the complete captured command timeline and final audits.
The captured transcript retains the obsolete original password from verbose FTP debugging, although direct evidence shows it was immediately rotated and the current handovers were synchronized.

There is no cluster subsystem in this topology; restart recovery evidence therefore covers each node's applicable services, files, security state, and end-to-end FTP workflow rather than cluster membership or resynchronization.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final hygiene is good: no failed units, package health remained sound, bounded temporary artifacts were removed, and the only new listener is the required node1 FTP service. Two unnecessary, bounded configuration mutations occurred: seccomp_sandbox=YES was added in the initial configuration, broke PASV, and was later removed; pasv_address was then temporarily removed as a troubleshooting experiment and restored after it did not help. Neither experiment remained. Additionally, verbose FTP debugging exposed the original password in captured output; the executor promptly rotated the password and synchronized both root-only handovers, so the exposed value was no longer current. The retained mode-0600 vendor configuration copy has a clear rollback purpose and is not treated as residue.
